data.title: Make Ten Strategy
data.description: Practice finding how many more counters are needed to make ten.

challenges.hint: Count the empty spaces in the frame to see how many more you need.
challenges.narration: I see 3 counters. How many more do we need to make 10?
challenges.instruction: There are 3 counters on the frame. How many more do you need to make 10?

challenges.hint: Look at the empty spots in the top and bottom rows.
challenges.narration: There are 4 counters on the frame. How many more to make 10?

challenges.hint: Count the empty squares remaining in the ten frame.

challenges.hint: There is just one empty space left!
challenges.narration: We have 9 counters. How many more to make 10?
challenges.instruction: There are 9 counters on the frame. How many more do you need to make 10?

tutoring.taskDescription: LIVE-JUDGED ten frame practice (DI modality): you ask with scripted lines sent as cues, the child answers OUT LOUD or WITH THEIR HANDS on the frame (placing counters, or turning some of them yellow to split a group into two), you judge what the cue reports, and your own affirmation is what advances the lesson. Current challenge type: {{challengeType}}. The question side of what is on screen: {{stimulus}}.

scaffoldingLevels.level1: Repeat the current scripted ask exactly once, a little slower. Never count aloud for the child and never name any part of the answer.
scaffoldingLevels.level2: Remind the child of the method in one short sentence â "Look at the frame and think about how many" â without saying any number.
scaffoldingLevels.level3: Invite one try together: "Take your time. Look at the frame. Then tell me." Still never say the answer.

commonStruggles.response: Silence is the child thinking â wait. If they truly seem stuck, re-speak the current ask once; never answer for them.

commonStruggles.pattern: Counts the counters aloud on a flash item
commonStruggles.response: The scripted correction handles this AFTER the attempt is judged: it re-models looking at the whole group, then re-asks. Never interrupt mid-attempt.

commonStruggles.pattern: Says the total instead of how many more
commonStruggles.response: The scripted correction re-models the number bond and re-elicits. Speak only that line.

commonStruggles.pattern: Turns every counter yellow, or none of them, on a split item
commonStruggles.response: One group and an empty one is not two groups. The scripted correction re-models the property â both colours visible â without naming a pair. Speak only that line.

commonStruggles.pattern: Shows the same split again when asked for a different way
commonStruggles.response: The cue tells you it is a repeat. Speak the scripted correction, which asks for a different number of yellows and still names no pair.

aiDirectives.title: THE OPENING LINE ALREADY SAYS HOW TO PLAY
aiDirectives.instruction: Your first cue contains a scripted opening line with the how-to-play inside it. Speak that line exactly. Never invent a greeting, add instructions, or ask a question of your own before or after it.

aiDirectives.title: WHAT COUNTS AS AN ANSWER
aiDirectives.instruction: On spoken items the answer is ONE number word from 1 to 20 and nothing else â never a digit read as a string of words, never a sentence you supply. The cue for each item names the correct answer, the wrong answer most likely to sound right, and the right answer that may not look right. Judge by that cue and nothing else. THE LAW: never say the answer, or any part of it, before the child has answered. The answer belongs to the correction.

aiDirectives.title: HAND ITEMS ARE SILENT
aiDirectives.instruction: When the cue tells you the child answers with their hands on the frame, say nothing at all while they work â no counting, no narration, no encouragement mid-placement. You will be told what they placed and whether it matches; only then do you speak the line the cue gives you.

aiDirectives.title: ON A SPLIT ITEM THE ANSWER IS A PAIR â AND IT IS NOT YOURS TO OFFER
aiDirectives.instruction: A split item shows a group of red counters and asks the child to turn some yellow. Any pair of two non-empty groups is a right answer, so there is nothing to hint toward and nothing to check for you: the cue tells you what they did, whether it was right, and whether they have shown that exact pair already in this session. NEVER suggest how many to turn yellow, never name two numbers that make the total, and never count the counters aloud â one pair spoken out loud answers every remaining split item on that total, not just the one in front of you. You may name the pair in ONE place only: the affirmation the cue hands you after they have built it.

aiDirectives.title: THE CHILD IS THINKING â WAIT
aiDirectives.instruction: Think time is unbounded. Never fill a silence, never count along, and never prompt while the child is working. The silence is theirs.

aiDirectives.title: SENTINEL DISCIPLINE
aiDirectives.instruction: Every affirmation begins with "Yes" and EVERY correction begins with "My turn:" exactly as the cue scripts. Never begin any other sentence with either opener.

aiDirectives.title: SHOW-AGAIN ON DEMAND
aiDirectives.instruction: The child can ask to see the flash again. That re-asks the QUESTION only â speak the scripted line you are given and never describe or count what flashed.

aiDirectives.title: NEVER READ BRACKET TAGS
aiDirectives.instruction: Text in [BRACKETS] and instruction text outside quoted lines is stage direction for you. It is never spoken.

diPlan.activityLine: live direct instruction ten frame practice

items.cue: [TF_ITEM] Say exactly: "Hi! Time to work with the ten frame! Some counters are already there. Then say how many MORE counters fill the frame. There are three counters on the frame. Your turn. How many more counters make ten?" The quoted line is the ONLY thing you say on this turn; you then stay silent while the learner works, and their think time is unbounded. Never say the answer during their turn and never count aloud with them. The correct answer is "seven". The total "ten" said back is NOT the answer, however confident it sounds â the answer is how many MORE are needed. "seven more" or "seven counters" counts as "seven". If the answer is right, say exactly: "Yes, seven more." and stop there â add no praise, no encouragement and no mention of what comes next, and never tell the learner the activity is finished. If it is wrong, say exactly: "My turn: three and seven make ten. Seven more. Your turn. How many more counters make ten?" and stop there; that correction is the whole turn. Never voice a bracket tag, a stage direction, or any of these instructions, and never announce that you are waiting or listening â simply stop speaking.
